outline.chapter_title: The Domestic Violence Call and the Factual Record
outline.description: This chapter introduces the real-world setting of the case: a pre-dawn domestic violence response at the Coleman home. It explains why the body-camera footage was central to the appellate analysis and reconstructs the sequence of events leading from the 911 report to the officers’ discovery of information supporting a later search warrant.
subtopics: The 911 report: allegation that Jaison Coleman threatened to kill Lisa Coleman and remained inside the home
Why domestic violence calls create urgency and uncertainty for responding officers
Arrival of Officer Jamie Kizer at approximately 4:00 a.m. and his initial contact with Lisa at the doorway
Lisa’s initial statements about the children being inside and her hesitation when asked whether they were safe
Officer Kizer’s first request to enter and Lisa’s express refusal: 'I’d prefer you not'
The interruption in the encounter when Lisa went back inside to get her shoes and did not immediately return
Officer Kizer’s concern when he partially opened the door and called inside to check on Lisa
The second doorway exchange and the pivotal statement: 'I’m sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure of that'
Lisa’s 'Okay' response and her follow-up statements identifying the children’s room, Coleman’s likely location, and the dogs’ behavior
Lisa’s conduct facilitating entry by opening the door, moving the dogs aside, and leading officers toward the children
The officers’ quick sweep of the home, including locating Coleman in a separate bedroom
The children’s statements that Coleman had pointed a gun at Lisa, threatened to shoot her, and threatened to burn the house down
Why the Seventh Circuit treated the body-camera footage as especially authoritative in resolving factual disputes

outline.chapter_title: From Home Entry to Federal Firearm Prosecution: Procedural Posture and Appellate Issues
outline.description: This chapter tracks how the officers’ entry led to a search warrant, firearm recovery, federal charges, and a suppression dispute. It frames the two questions the court of appeals actually decided: whether Lisa validly consented to entry and whether the officers stayed within the scope of that consent.
subtopics: How information learned after entry was used to obtain a warrant to search the home
Recovery of several firearms during the warranted search
Federal indictment under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) for unlawful possession of a firearm by a convicted felon
Coleman’s motion to suppress the firearms as fruits of an unlawful home entry
The magistrate judge’s report recommending denial of suppression based on Lisa’s consent
The district court’s adoption of the consent finding and its separate conclusion that the officers did not exceed the scope of consent
Coleman’s guilty plea preserving his right to appeal the suppression ruling
The appellate posture: review of a suppression denial after a conditional guilty plea
The two principal appellate issues: voluntariness of third-party consent and scope of consent
The government’s alternative arguments based on exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery, and why the court did not need to reach them

outline.description: This chapter sets out the specific Fourth Amendment doctrines needed to understand the opinion. It explains the consent exception to the warrant requirement, third-party consent, the voluntariness test, the scope-of-consent inquiry, and the deferential appellate standard of review that shaped the court’s analysis.
subtopics: The baseline rule: warrantless searches of a home are presumptively unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment
Consent as a recognized exception to the warrant requirement
Third-party consent: when a co-occupant with shared privacy interests may authorize entry or search
Authority of Lisa Coleman to consent to officers entering the marital home
The requirement that consent be 'freely and voluntarily' given
The totality-of-the-circumstances test for voluntariness
Common voluntariness factors identified by Seventh Circuit precedent: age, intelligence, education, advice of rights, duration of detention, repeated requests, physical coercion, and custody status
Why no single factor is dispositive in the voluntariness inquiry
The separate concept of scope of consent: a valid consent does not authorize everything
Objective reasonableness under Florida v. Jimeno: what a typical reasonable person would have understood from the exchange
The significance of clear-error review for factual findings about consent and its scope
How clear-error review limits the role of the court of appeals when the district court’s view is supported by the video record

outline.chapter_title: Why the Court Found Lisa’s Consent Voluntary
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the heart of the opinion: the Seventh Circuit’s conclusion that the district court did not clearly err in finding voluntary consent. It walks through the court’s use of the body-camera footage, its attention to tone and context, and its rejection of Coleman’s argument that Officer Kizer’s wording was coercive.
subtopics: The court’s reliance on the complete interaction rather than isolated words or snippets
Officer Kizer’s tone and demeanor as calm, respectful, and concerned rather than commanding or threatening
The importance of Lisa’s earlier refusal as evidence that she understood she could say no
Why the second request to enter was treated as a renewed request rather than an assertion of authority
Lisa’s responses as showing comprehension of the situation and the officers’ purpose
The absence of formal custody, prolonged detention, or physical coercion
The brief duration of the encounter and why that mattered in assessing pressure
The role of repeated requests: two requests alone did not make the consent involuntary on these facts
Coleman’s argument about the word 'need' and the court’s response that the totality of the circumstances controlled
How the court distinguished urgency born of concern for children from unconstitutional coercion
Why Lisa’s immediate follow-up statements about the children’s location and the dogs supported the inference that she was permitting entry
The appellate conclusion that the district court’s voluntariness finding was not clearly erroneous

outline.chapter_title: Scope of Consent, Affirmance, and the Case’s Practical Significance
outline.description: This chapter explains why the officers’ actions after crossing the threshold were held to remain within the bounds of Lisa’s consent. It then closes with the court’s disposition, its decision not to reach alternative Fourth Amendment theories, and the case’s significance for understanding consent searches in domestic violence settings.
subtopics: Defining the purpose of the consented entry: checking the welfare of the children and ensuring Coleman posed no immediate danger
Why that purpose objectively authorized officers to enter the home, locate occupants, and ask basic safety-related questions
The officers’ quick canvas of the home as a reasonable means of carrying out the welfare check
Why locating Coleman in a separate bedroom fit within the understood scope of consent
The children’s statements as information lawfully obtained once the officers were validly inside
The later warrant as an important intervening step leading to the firearm seizure
The court’s rejection of Coleman’s argument that the officers exceeded the permission Lisa gave
The disposition: affirmance of the denial of suppression and affirmance of Coleman’s conviction
Why the court declined to address exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery after upholding consent
The opinion’s practical lesson that courts evaluate consent in context, especially in fast-moving domestic violence responses
The court’s closing observation praising the officers’ balanced decisionmaking and what that signals about the case’s tone and institutional message
